cues.text: The Social Question
By the late nineteenth century, the Industrial Revolution had transformed working life across Europe and America.

It concentrated vast wealth among factory owners, while masses of laborers endured long hours, dangerous conditions, and meager wages, often uprooted from traditional rural communities into crowded industrial cities.
Socialism offered one answer to this 'social question,' proposing the abolition of private property; unregulated capitalism offered another, trusting market forces alone.
Leo XIII's Intervention
Pope Leo XIII drew on Catholic social thinkers such as Cardinal Gaspard Mermillod's Fribourg Union and bishops including Cardinal James Gibbons in America.
He issued the encyclical Rerum Novarum ('Of New Things') on May 15, 1891 , subtitled 'On the Condition of Labor.'
It was the Church's first major, systematic engagement with the industrial economic order.
A Middle Way
Leo firmly rejected socialism's proposed abolition of private property as unjust and contrary to natural law, while equally condemning the exploitation of workers under unregulated capitalism.
He insisted that a just wage must allow a working man to support himself and his family in reasonable comfort.
He wrote that if a worker "accept harder conditions because an employer or contractor will afford him no better, he is made the victim of force and injustice."
Rights and Duties on All Sides
The encyclical laid out mutual obligations: the state's duty to protect workers' rights and promote the common good without absorbing all property into itself.
It affirmed employers' duty to pay fair wages and provide safe conditions, and workers' right to form associations and unions to defend their interests.
This position gave crucial Church encouragement to the nascent Catholic labor movement in many countries.
Immediate Reception

The encyclical drew both praise and criticism: some economic liberals faulted its skepticism of unregulated markets, and some socialists, including the American economist Henry George, wrote extended public rebuttals defending broader property reforms.
Nonetheless, it quickly became a foundational reference point for Catholic social and labor movements across Europe and North America in the following decades.
Legacy
Rerum Novarum is universally regarded as the founding document of modern Catholic social teaching , inaugurating a tradition of papal social encyclicals.
That tradition continued through Pius XI's Quadragesimo Anno (1931, its fortieth anniversary), John XXIII's Mater et Magistra, John Paul II's Centesimus Annus (its centenary, 1991), and beyond.
These encyclicals established principles of subsidiarity, solidarity, and the dignity of labor that remain central to Catholic engagement with economic life today.
